1.	Yes.

The undersigned, in concluding his memorandum on the subject of government ownership of railways, would wish to make a short reference to the project now in contemplation by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, or the leading parties connected with that corporation. Since the undersigned first called the attention of his colleagues^to the necessity of devising some other method of ensuring the railway development of sections of the country needing railway accommodation, other than by bonus-ing or subsidizing companies, public opinion has made vast strides and is now very decidedly opposed to the policy, at least, on any large scale, or in respect of important lines which promise to become self-paying undertakings. Assistance in some form or another, it is alleged, must be given if railway needs are to be supplied, and assuming this to be the case, the question is : How shall assistance be rendered ? The undersigned has been of opinion that there are only two methods of assisting companies, in the case of such railways as have been alluded to, which would be seriously considered. One is by way of loan, payment being secured by mortgage upon the railway undertaking-the amount being limited to such sum as is required to put the railway in good working condition after taking into account the capital actually subscribed and paid in, and any sum borrowed on a first mortgage. Such a method would call for very careful supervision of the company's expenditure on construction and equipment, and would necessitate the taking of a second mortgage as security for the government loan. And it would be expected that only such enterprises should be aided in this way as would be likely to ultimately repay both principal and interest.
The other method would be by guarantee of the company's second mortgage bonds. This plan involves the same care and supervision as the first. While either of these alternative modes of aiding railway enterprises is to be preferred to the gift of a bonus or subsidy, even they are not free from grave objections.

The statement is made-deliberately made and repeated-that the country is incurring liabilities in respect of this enterprise for the advantage of the Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk Pacific of from 150 to 170 million dollars. The impression is conveyed that the liabilities of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and of the government in connection with this enterprise, are respectively 15 and 150 million dollars. This is practically an absolute reversal of the facts. The case is such as that of a citizen, who with a lot, a thousand dollars in cash and a well established and paying business, undertakes to build a ten thousand dollar house. He puts in his thousand dollars, the loan company advances him nine thousand dollars, and takes a mortgage upon the completed house as security for principal and interest. Is the loan company assuming a liability for $10,000 or is the debtor assuming that liability ? If the debtor does not pay, the company gets his thousand dollars and the house. The risk, and therefore the liability is his, not that of the loan company. If the Grand Trunk Pacific does not pay interest on that part of the cost of the road contributed, or guaranteed by the government, the Grand Trunk loses control of the road, and the Grand Trunk Pacific loses any return on the proceeds of the $45,000,000 of preferred and common stock which it is allowed to issue. The government takes control of the road and becomes absolute owner of twenty million dollars worth of rolling stock supplied by the company with which to operate it. Both country and company go into the project in the belief that the traffic will pay interest on the cost ; but if that expectation fails, the company, not the country, loses its investment.

I beg to call your attention and the attention of the House to the proposal of the hon. leader of the opposition. His proposal is to extend the Intercolonial to Depot Harbour, and I suppose on from that to Winnipeg, buying the Canada Atlantic line and the Canadian Pacific line, and building westward from Winnipeg. These railways are to be bought this year. If they sell, they will expect to be paid immediately. If they are to be paid immediately, the interest to be paid on the purchase money would be at four percent.
Now assuming the cost from Moncton to Winnipeg to be $65,000,000, and allowing seven years' interest, during which the Grand Trunk Pacific pays no rent, that, at 3i per cent, would amount to $2,270,000 per annum, or, for the seven years, $16,000,000. That would bring up the total cost to $81,000,000. Then, for the Quebec bridge I will allow a cost of $6,700,000, and interest amounting to $300,000, making in all $7,000,000. It was argued very cogently and successfully by my hon. friend from Haldimand <Mr. A. T. Thompson) that two or three railways would participate in the use. of that bridge and would -contribute to its cost by way of either interest or tolls ; so that the sums derived for the use of that bridge would pay the interest on the original cost, and the issue of bonds or other securities for the amount would be simply so much paper, while the interest was being paid to the government.
For the prairie section of 1,000 miles it is fair to assume that nothing is to be paid. On that point Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson further said :
As regards the prairie section, the government, not unfairly, held that it would be selfsustaining from the day of its completion, and in this view we are willing to concur.

Third. A foreclosure in case of default of interest ,-to be paid by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. I am not a lawyer, and have no intimate acquaintance with the mode of foreclosure. I do not wish to add to the learned legal argument made on this question. It has been thoroughly elucidated. My- effort would not tend to cast further light upon it. but rather to obscure it. But there was one singular remark made upon this subject by the leader of the opposition. That remark was to the effect that if this portion of the road should prove unremunerative the Grand Trunk Pacific Company would make default, in * which case the road might be. put in the hands of a receiver ; but when business revived and traffic increased, making the road profitable, then /the Grand Trunk Pacific Company would take the road
back and operate it during the good times ;_
and, I suppose, they would leave it to the government again when the profits fell off. I may be bold enough to say that if there be any suspicion in the minds of the leader of the opposition or auy other gentleman that this kind of sliding scale could be put in force, the matter should be made clear. It would not be creditable to the government of Canada that there should be any such alternating of control. Once default is made ror a number of years, after due charity has been extended to the undertaking, if it is found that either wilfully or by reason of inability, the company does i/ot work that section of the road, the government should resume possession of it and operate it for -ill time.
Fourth. Alteration in the contract as to the common stock of $25,000,000 to be handed over to the Grand Trunk. Part of that item, I have no doubt, was to provide rolling-stock, part was for ships and part for other expense, perhaps to provide the balance of capital between what the government would supply and that which the Grand Trunk . Company would have to furnish on the two sections. But the learned leader of the opposition goes on to say that these are con-

conveying of Russian troops and munitions of war over Lake Baikal because be said that navigation might be prolonged a little longer in the fall of the year by ice breakers. I would like to see the commerce of the great lakes, the commerce of the great west, the commerce which goes to the maritime provinces depending upon the water being kept open in a winter like the last one by ice breakers on Lake Superior or any other lake. How would it be in winter along the projected Grand Trunk Pacific Railway? The winter of 1004 will long be remembered in Canada and the northern states on account for the severe weather and continuous snow storms which blocked the railways almost everywhere and especially in western Ontario to an extent without precedent in railway experience, some of the lines being closed for weeks at a time and on this we are to depend to carry out the project of the hon. leader of the opposition. The following editorial from the Toronto ' Globe ' on March 3, 1904, shows that northern Quebec, usually looked upon as the region of snow blockades is not so white as it is painted, the most northern railway in the province not having cancelled a single train -freight or passenger-during this exceptional winter, and its tonnage hauled showing increases every week since December last:
The Unblockaded North.
The man with the yardstick is reporting on the snow blockade. Bight feet on the level is a customary figure, but one observer, with a talent for accuracy, announces that the depth in his locality is thirteen feet three inches. Snow stories are the winter counterpart of fish stories in summer. Amid all this talk of the blockade it is pleasant to learn of some part of the country where the snowfall does not interfere with traffic, and, curiously enough, the north country furnishes It. It is now about ten years since the Quebec and Lake St. John Railway was completed from Quebec to Roberval and Chicoutimi, a distance of 240 miles, traversing a portion of the same country, northwest of Quebec, through which the government Pacific road is to pass. During all these years this road has been operated without any interruption whatever from snow. The Quebec papers tell us that during this exceptional winter and through all the storms of this northern country the Lake St. John passenger trains have been running sharp on time, there has been no delay in the freight service, and the earnings show satisfactory increases over last winter. The road has been sending all winter thousands of tons of pulp from the mills of the north to the paper mills in New England, which, owing to the scarcity of water, they cannot get from the pulp mills in their own country.
There is a good argument in all this for the new transcontinental. It shows the wisdom of the government's decision to build the road by the shortest and most direct line from Quebec to Winnipeg, north of the height of land in the James Bay territory of Quebec and Ontario. The objection has- been raised that it might be difficult to operate such a road in the winter owing to the excessive snowfall.
